item.title: [Retailing 101 #7] Trader Joe's Sells 4,000 Items. Walmart Sells 100,000. Both Are Winning.
item.body:
> A retail strategy is three decisions made together: who you're for, what you'll sell them and how, and why that edge will still be there in five years.

## Today's Concept

Most people think retail strategy means "pick a good location and don't get undercut on price." That's tactics. Strategy is the layer above it.

In retailing textbooks, a **retail strategy** is a statement that answers three questions:

1. **Target market** — which customers are we aiming at?
2. **Retail format** — what offering will we build to serve them?
3. **Sustainable competitive advantage** — what will make that hard for rivals to copy?

The word *sustainable* is doing real work in question 3. Any competitor can match your Tuesday discount by Wednesday. Advantages that actually last tend to come from a small set of places: customer loyalty and habit, physical locations rivals can't get, unique merchandise you control, distribution and information systems, supplier relationships, and how you hire and keep staff. A price cut isn't on that list.

The format in question 2 gets built out of the **retail mix** — the six levers a retailer pulls, all of which have to point the same direction:

- **Merchandise assortment** — how many categories (breadth), how many choices inside each (depth)
- **Pricing** — everyday low price, high-low promotion, premium
- **Location** — mall, strip center, downtown, online-only
- **Store design and display** — layout, atmosphere, how much you can carry in one hand
- **Customer service** — staffed help desk vs. self-checkout vs. chat bot
- **Communication** — advertising, email, loyalty programs, social

Set those six, and you've produced a **position**: the place your store occupies in a shopper's head relative to the alternatives. Positioning isn't a slogan you write. It's the residue of the six choices you actually made.

The uncomfortable part is that the mix has to be *internally consistent*. Deep assortment plus low prices plus high service plus prime real estate is not a strategy — it's a wish list, and it loses money. Every strong retailer is visibly bad at something on purpose.

## In Everyday Life

Say you live in Columbus, Ohio, and there are four grocery options within a fifteen-minute drive. Same city, same shoppers, four completely different answers.

**Trader Joe's** carries roughly 4,000 items. A conventional supermarket carries 30,000 or more. Most of what's on a TJ's shelf is its own private label, there's no loyalty card, no weekly circular, and stores are small — often in older, cheaper retail space rather than a new anchor pad. Notice the consistency: a narrow assortment means high volume per item, which means better cost per unit, which funds a $3.99 price on something that feels specialty. Their advantage is unique merchandise you literally cannot buy elsewhere, plus a store small enough that a full trip takes twenty minutes. Target market: shoppers who'd rather have someone else edit the choices for them.

**Aldi**, two miles away, is stricter still. Products stay in the shipping carton, you rent the cart with a quarter, you bag your own groceries and bring your own bags. Every one of those is a cost removed and passed into price. Target: shoppers whose top priority is the total at the bottom of the receipt.

**Walmart Supercenter** goes the opposite way — enormous assortment, groceries plus tires plus TVs, everyday low price funded not by a small assortment but by supply chain and information systems built over decades. That's an advantage measured in billions of dollars of infrastructure, which is exactly why it's sustainable.

**Whole Foods** charges more and is fine with that: prepared foods, staffed counters, sourcing standards, locations in higher-income trade areas.

Now the key point. None of these four is "the best grocery store," and none is trying to beat the others at their own game. Trader Joe's isn't losing when Walmart has a bigger cereal aisle — a narrow aisle is the strategy. When a retailer *does* try to be all four at once, the mix goes incoherent, the position blurs, and shoppers stop being able to say what the store is for. That's the usual autopsy on a failed chain.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Retail strategy = target market + retail format + a competitive advantage that's actually hard to copy.
2. The format is built from six mix levers — assortment, price, location, design, service, communication — and they must be consistent with each other.
3. Positioning is the result of those choices in the customer's mind; being deliberately weak in some areas is what makes you strong in others.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** Which of the following is generally the *least* sustainable source of competitive advantage in retail?
A. Prime locations competitors can't obtain
B. A price cut on a nationally branded product
C. Proprietary private-label merchandise
D. A distribution and information system built over decades

**Q2.** O/X — A retailer can simultaneously offer the deepest assortment, the lowest prices, and the highest service level, as long as it works hard enough.

**Q3.** In the retail mix, "breadth" refers to:
A. The number of different categories carried
B. The number of choices within a single category
C. The physical square footage of the store
D. The size of the advertising budget

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Retail strategy** — A statement of the retailer's target market, the format it will use to serve that market, and the basis of its sustainable competitive advantage.
- **Target market** — The specific customer segment a retailer directs its resources and retail mix toward.
- **Retail format** — The nature of the retailer's offering, defined by its mix of assortment, price, location, design, service, and communication.
- **Retail mix** — The six controllable levers a retailer combines to build that format.
- **Positioning** — The image a retailer occupies in customers' minds relative to competitors, produced by its retail mix.
- **Sustainable competitive advantage** — An edge that can be maintained over time because rivals can't easily replicate it.

---

*Answers: **Q1 → B.** A price cut is the easiest move in retail to copy — a competitor can match it the next morning, so it buys volume, not advantage. Locations, proprietary merchandise, and supply-chain infrastructure all take years and capital to replicate. **Q2 → X (False).** Each element of the mix has a cost; deep assortment and high service raise the cost structure, which makes the lowest price impossible to sustain. Coherent strategy requires choosing what to be weak at. **Q3 → A.** Breadth (or variety) = number of categories; depth = number of SKUs within a category. Trader Joe's is moderate in breadth and deliberately shallow in depth.*
